newsitem.title: EGYPT: Velayati says better Iran, Egypt links beneficial.
newsitem.headline: Velayati says better Iran, Egypt links beneficial.

text.p: Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati said on Monday problems facing the Middle East would benefit from better ties between his country and Egypt, which charges Tehran with trying to kill President Hosni Mubarak.

Speaking briefly to reporters on the first high-level visit by an Iranian official to Cairo since 1994, Velayati described his talks with Egyptian counterpart Amr Moussa as "very friendly" and said that cooperation would help solve complicated problems like the deadlock in the Middle East peace process.
"We do believe that cooperation between Iran and Egypt would be very constructive," Velayati said after more than two hours of formal talks with Moussa.

"This cooperation would be beneficial to the Islamic umma (nation) as a whole specifically during these days where the Islamic world is facing some problems and there are some very complicated problems...like the situation of Palestine and the situation in the Middle East," he added.
Israeli-Palestinian peace talks are suspended over Israel's decision to build a controversial Jewish settlement in disputed Arab East Jerusalem.
Velayati said that he would also give to Mubarak on Tuesday a handwritten invitation by Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani to an Islamic summit in Tehran in December.

Ties between Egypt and Iran have been strained for years over policy differences but some analysts say that Tehran is trying to win over Cairo after a diplomatic row with European Union, its main trading partner.
Relations between Iran and the EU plummeted after a German court ruled that Iran had ordered the 1992 killings of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin. Tehran denies the charge.
The 15-nation bloc temporarily withdrew its ambassadors from Tehran after the April 10 court verdict and then decided last week to send the envoys back.

The EU, however, suspended ministerial contacts with Tehran and Iranian officials reacted to the EU decisions by saying they too have frozen all ties with the bloc and that they would not allow the German ambassador to return for now.

"My visit to Egypt will be a chance to exchange views on a number of Islamic problems and there is no doubt that when contacts increase between the two countries it will help create a better atmosphere," Velayati told reporters at Cairo airport.

Egypt has accused Iran and Sudan of continuing support for the al-Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), the largest organisation fighting to set up a strict Islamic state in Egypt. Both Sudan and Iran deny this.
Asked to comment on charges that Iran was aiding militants in Egypt, Velayati said: "This is not true. Iran does not support any terrorist groups. It does not and will not aid such organisations".
Iran was also accused of being behind the attempted assassination of Mubarak during the Egyptian leader's visit to Ethiopia in 1995.
Velayati last visited Cairo in 1994 to attend a Non-Aligned Movement meeting of foreign ministers.
